lede: Before you change a table, look at it: which columns it has, what type each one is, how many rows there are and what the values look like. A DataFrame can tell you all of that in a line or two.
objectives: Read a DataFrame's columns and types with `printSchema()`, `columns`, `dtypes` and `schema`
Print rows with `show(n)`, and in full with `truncate=False`
Count rows and fetch the first ones with `count()`, `first()` and `head(n)`

blocks.md:
In every example on this page the shop's `orders` table is loaded as a DataFrame called `orders`.

`printSchema()` prints the table's **schema**: every column, its type, and whether it may be missing (`nullable`). `columns` gives just the names, as a plain Python list.

blocks.title: Columns and their types
blocks.note: Six columns. `order_date` is a real date and `total` an exact amount with two decimal places, not text.

blocks.md: When your code needs the types, use `dtypes`: a list of `(name, type)` pairs, with the type written the way you'd write it in a schema string. `schema` is the full description, one `StructField` per column. Lesson 13 looks at it closely.

blocks.title: Types in code
blocks.note: `dict(orders.dtypes)` lets you look up a column's type by its name. `schema["order_date"]` gives that column's name, type and whether it may be missing (`True`).

blocks.title: Calling a property
blocks.note: `columns`, `dtypes` and `schema` are properties: write them without brackets. `printSchema()`, `show()` and `count()` are methods, so they need the brackets.

blocks.md: `show()` prints the first 20 rows. Give it a number to print fewer. It also cuts any value longer than 20 characters and ends it with `...`, so the table stays narrow; `show(truncate=False)` prints every value in full.

blocks.title: A few rows, and long text in full
blocks.code:
orders.show(3)

notes = spark.createDataFrame([("O00001", "Leave the parcel with the neighbour at number 12")], "order_id STRING, note STRING")
notes.show()
notes.show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: `show(3)` prints three rows and says it's only showing the top ones. The note is cut to 20 characters the first time and printed in full the second.

blocks.md:
`count()` counts the rows and gives back a Python number. `first()` gives back the first row as a `Row`, and `head(n)` a list of up to `n` rows. You can read a value from a `Row` by its column name.

The tables haven't been sorted, so "first" just means the first row Spark comes to; for these small tables that's the first line of the file. Lesson 11 shows how to sort.

blocks.title: Count rows and look at the first ones
blocks.code:
print(orders.count())

first = orders.first()
print(first)
print(first["status"], first["total"])

print(len(orders.head(5)))
blocks.note: In Python, the date comes back as a `date` and the amount as a `Decimal`, the same kinds of value you used to build DataFrames in lesson 7.

blocks.md: For a quick feel of the numbers, `describe()` works out the count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum of each column. `summary()` does the same and can add percentiles like `"50%"` (the median); you can name just the ones you want. Both give back a small DataFrame, so you `show()` it.

blocks.title: Quick statistics
blocks.note: Text columns get a count and their alphabetically first and last values, but no median, so that cell is `NULL`. Date columns like `order_date` are left out.

concept.prompt: Which line prints how many rows `orders` has?
concept.why: `count()` is a method: with the brackets it counts the rows. Without them you print the method itself, and `len(orders.columns)` counts columns.

choices: A list of (name, type) pairs, one per column
A list of the column names only
A method you have to call: `orders.dtypes()`
concept.why: `dtypes` is a property that holds a list like `[('order_id', 'string'), ...]`. `columns` has the names only, and `describe()` gives statistics.

concept.prompt: A text value is 30 characters long. What does `df.show()` print for it?
concept.why: `show()` keeps each value to 20 characters: 17 of the text and `...`. Use `show(truncate=False)` to see it all.

review: `printSchema()` prints each column, its type and whether it may be missing.
`columns` is a list of names and `dtypes` a list of `(name, type)` pairs. They're properties: no brackets.
`show(n)` prints the first `n` rows (20 by default) and cuts long values; `show(truncate=False)` prints them in full.
`count()` counts the rows. `first()` gives one `Row` and `head(n)` a list of up to `n` rows.
`describe()` and `summary()` give quick statistics as a small DataFrame; `summary` can add percentiles.
Without sorting, "first" just means the first row Spark comes to.
